newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Britain, Swiss seek to patch up row over Nazi gold.
newsitem.headline: Britain, Swiss seek to patch up row over Nazi gold.

text.p: Britain and Switzerland on Wednesday sought to patch up any disagreements following British government allegations that the Swiss returned only one-tenth of Nazi gold demanded by the Allies after World War Two.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said he welcomed Swiss government efforts to clear up the fate of the gold.
"I very much welcome the announcement that was made by Swiss federal authorities earlier this week on setting up the comprehensive study into this question," Rifkind told a news conference.

Switzerland is confronting allegations that its banks, including its central bank, played a big role in helping Nazi Germany to stash and launder valuables, including gold plundered from its victims and the countries it invaded.
Both Rifkind and his Swiss counterpart, Flavio Cotti, said after holding talks that they would wait until all the facts were established before making pronouncements on the issues.
Their talks included Berne's plans for a commission of experts to study the extent and fate of both Nazi and Jewish riches deposited in neutral Switzerland during World War Two.
Cotti told the joint news conference he was confident that the Swiss parliament would give final backing to legislation creating the historical commission after the cabinet backed the bill on Monday.
He said the commission's work "has only one goal, to make definitely clear the situation during the Second World War.

"If you ask me about the facts at this time, I wouldn't be able to answer. It (the commission study) is a historical research. The consequences of this study will be presented to the Federal Council," Cotti said.
"We have to make history precise, and after that, we will take decisions," he added.
Rifkind called the commission on wartime wealth and Swiss banking an "appropriate and sensitive response. I very much welcome that response."

A British Foreign Office report last week increased pressure on Swiss leaders to counter speculation that Nazi gold was still hidden in the country's central bank. It revived allegations that the Swiss kept nearly nine-tenths of gold bought from Hitler's Germany.
The Swiss National Bank has acknowledged that it was too trusting of Germany in buying 1.2 billion Swiss francs (about $300 million at 1946 exchange rates) worth of gold between 1938 and 1945.
Several questions remain regarding the gold, including the precise amount. One, for example, is whether the amounts cited are dollars or Swiss francs.
"That is precisely one of the issues the investigation will look at and come to conclusion on," Rifkind said.
Rifkind, saying that Britain's relationship with Switzerland was "superbly healthy", underlined Switzerland's neutral status during World War Two.
"One recollects the way in which Switzerland during the war years was a beacon for liberty and freedom, surrounded as it was by totalitarian dark forces," Rifkind said.

Switzerland has said all legal obligations for the return of Nazi gold had been settled by a 1946 agreement with the Allied powers to pay them a settlement of 250 million Swiss francs (about $60 million at the time).
